audits.title: Food of non-animal origin in the retail sector

recommendations.text: General guidelines of the national food control programme should be followed. More detailed guidance in food control should be established and communicated at the municipal food control authorities.
Written reports should be produced after every visit.They should be sent to the food operator and should be kept on file.
Food operators should be encouraged to document the scope of their in-house control which will ensure that all products handled, stored or prepared on the premises are covered.
The consistent application of in-house control among food operators should be taken of particular attention by the competent authorities.
The pest and insect control in food premises has to be evaluated and a programme has to be created for it.

The competent authority should ensure that on going training is provided to at least one health inspector per municipality so that all municipal environmental health units participate in some training session every year and create a system to identify and register training needs centrally. 25
The hygiene standards for old premises should be evaluated and a programme of improvement should be put in place to reach the required standards and to meet the current regulations.
Within 6 months from the dispatch of this report the competent authority should provide a programme that corresponds to these recommendations.
The competent authorities of Finland should take appropriate action to rectify the deficiencies referred to under the different conclusions in Section 5 above.

The competent authorities of Finland should take appropriate action to rectify the deficiencies found in the establishments visited and any deficiencies of the same type in all the other approved establishments in Finland.

Within three months after the receipt of the final report the competent authorities of Finland should inform the Commission of the progress and result of the measures taken including a timetable for completion of measures and actions still outstanding at that time. PAGE 29 ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)1160/2000 Competent Authority's (CA) response to the recommendations in the report The CA has stated, in their letter of 30 October 2000, that the following actions have been or will be taken to rectify the shortcomings indicated during the FVO inspection: · The EELA will ask the Provincial State Offices and municipal food control authorities to ensure that the use of health marks is adequate in all establishments in order to guarantee that raw materials originating from low capacity establishments may not be labelled with EC health marks. Measures have already been taken in the meat product plant that obviously had not operated in compliance with the legislation. · The numbers of official veterinarians will be increased to guarantee that the official veterinarian is full time present during the working hours in slaughterhouses. Also the number of auxiliaries will be checked and increased where necessary. · The supervision of establishments and the enforcement processes have been discussed with the official veterinarians and further education on the subject is going to be arranged also in the future. · Most of the shortcomings noticed during the mission in the establishments have already been corrected or are going to be corrected in very near future. · Official veterinarians are instructed more in detail on how to record the checks of flock records and hygienic standards etc. during farm visits. · The legislation concerning Salmonella control will be reviewed by the end of the year in order to set the interval of official sampling at hatcheries to 8 weeks. Also the responsibilities of official veterinarians in supervision and in official sampling will be redefined and the rules on sanctions strengthened. The supervision of Salmonella control in Åland Islands will be reinforced. · The official veterinarians in slaughterhouses have been instructed to carry out the checks of transport of poultry on a regularly basis and to document these checks. The official veterinarians have also been instructed to document the checks of stunning in an appropriate way. · The Provincial State Offices have been instructed to take measures to ensure that the veterinarians responsible for performing the inspections on laying hen farms receive adequate training and assistance for there duties in practise. The CA had already stated, in their letter of 14 July 2000, that some of the severe shortcomings noticed in one establishment visited during the FVO inspection have been rectified already and that the remaining ones will be rectified soon. recommendations.text: To issue instructions for provincial veterinary officers clearly indicating their tasks and responsibilities ensuring a proper monitoring and supervision in relation with the active surveillance programme and the specified risk material. All tools should be made available to them (e.g. testing results, data on fallen stock collected and sampled) in order to allow a correct fulfilment of their tasks. 8.1.2. With regards to the epidemio-surveillance

Assurance should be given as matter of urgency that the application of the health marks used in fresh meat establishments is fully under the control of the competent authorities. A permanent official control of all fresh meat establishments should be ensured as well as a constant monitoring in place to guarantee the eligibility of the animals (control of age) and that cut meat having the Community health mark is derived from carcasses of the same health status.

To regularly control the system in place concerning the eligibility of bovines to be tested and in particular the age of the animals at slaughterhouse and rendering plant level. Moreover laboratory results should be sent directly to the competent authority, which should perform cross-checks on the animals tested and the laboratory results received. 34
To ensure that all parts of the body of sampled bovines are retained under official supervision until a negative result is available.
To ensure that all samples are taken and processed without unnecessary delay. 8.1.3. With regards to the feeding of processed animal proteins

To ensure that transport and storage of sacked feed materials destined to ruminants in plants using derogated processed animal proteins is completely separated from feed material prohibited for feeding to ruminants as laid down in the Annex I point 6 first indent of Commission Decision 2001/9/EC.
To ensure that other checks during the inspections e.g. documentary or identity checks should also be documented after the on spot visits.
To issue instructions on how to select farms to be inspected and sampled. Controls should be more targeted on mobile mixers and home compounders using fishmeal.
To apply the authorisation requirements of Annex I point 6 of Commission Decision 2001/9/EC on mobile mixers and home compounders using fishmeal.
To consider implementing a system of control/channelling of meat and bone meal produced in the two rendering plants. 8.1.4. With regards to Specified Risk Material
To use clearly identifiable containers for the collection and transport of SRM.

A control system/Reconciliation of SRM throughout the whole chain from removal to storage should be applied. In order to achieve this the central competent authorities should consider issuing instructions for the different services involved.

To ensure that storage of SRM-MBM are fully under official control, furthermore a solution should be considered to ensure safe disposal of these materials. 35 9. ADDENDUM TO THE MISSION REPORT Competent Authority response to the recommendations in the report. The Finnish authorities stated in their comments that: With regards to the follow up of the previous mission 1. Written instructions shall be sent to all PVOs by the end of September describing all their duties concerning the supervision of the epidemio-surveillance and SRM. With regards to the epidemio-surveillance 2. The measures taken in this field have been reviewed in autumn 2000 and spring 2001. In addition to this, the use of the health mark and the connection between the health marks used in carcasses and in cut meat thereof is clarified by a new Statute on Meat Hygiene (16/EEO/2001), which came into force 23rd of April this year. 3. All the results of the active surveillance shall be sent directly from the laboratory to the PVOs for supervision from 15.9.2001. All the forms except those of fallen stock accompanying the samples have been sent to the PVOs already since July for control purposes. Instructions concerning cross-checking of the age of animals at slaughterhouses shall be sent to the PVOs by the end of September. 4. All parts of sampled animals are now retained under official control. 5. The situation concerning the possible delay between taking samples and processing in the laboratory has been improved. With regards to the feeding of processed animal proteins 6. Instructions have already been sent to the relevant feed plant in order to arrange that the sacked feed materials destined for ruminants are stored separately from feed for other purposes. 7. Mobile mixers using fishmeal are already approved and controlled in the same way as industrial feed compounding, and there are also detailed control instructions for farms. In the future controls will be targeted on mixed farms using protein concentrate containing fishmeal. Instructions have been sent (August 2001) to the inspectors of Employment and Economic Development Centres. With regards to Specified Risk Material 8. A circular letter dated on 6.9.2001 has been sent to the slaughterhouses and their veterinary officers concerning the clear and definite separation of different categories of animal waste at any time. At the same time detailed instructions were given for the cross-checking of SRM. 9. Instructions on control of removal of SRM will be given by NFA during autumn 2001. 10. Detailed instructions have been given to MVOs supervising the storage of pre- processed SRM in a letter dated on 6.9. 2001. Also keys to the storages have been 36 delivered to the MVO's in July so that they can independently at any time check the storage of MBM. An official working group has been established in order to find out a solution for the final destruction of the stored SRM in Finland and this working group shall start its work in Mid-September 2001. 37

audits.title: Control systems for placing on the market and use of plant protection products and for residues in foodstuffs of plant origin

recommendations.text: The competent authorities of Finland should ensure that appropriate corrective measures are taken in respect of infringements found as a result of controls on the marketing and use of plant protection products.
The competent authorities of Finland should ensure that the labels of plant protection products placed on the market are controlled as required by article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC.
The competent authorities of Finland should ensure that all samples for pesticide residue analyses are taken randomly throughout the lot and that the sample bags are sealed.

The competent authorities of Finland should ensure that any information relating to a pesticide residue risk to human health are notified to the Commission under the rapid alert system according to Regulation (EC) N° 178/2002 of the European Parliament and the Council. An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation. 8. To take the necessary measures to organise real time alert and simulation exercises including all the people that should be involved in an outbreak.
To develop possible disease scenarios (single outbreak to worst case scenarios) for CSF and FMD and to use their results to validate and improve the CPs at national and provincial level.

audits.title: Illegal Imports of products of animal origin and live animals

recommendations.text: Background Customs are responsible for personal luggage checks of travellers in all points of entry. They check all points of entry including checks in the main mail centre at Helsinki airport. An annually organised specific one week training including restrictions for imports of live animals and products of animal origin is provided for staff from each customs district. This training also includes in-depth CITES issues.

Information to passengers/travellers Posters, in three or four different languages, have been submitted by VBI to all entry points. An overview, whether posters had been displayed, was available based on the feedback from the entry points requested by VBI. However, on the spot, the posters displayed in the entry points visited do not always contain all the information foreseen in Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. Leaflets, prepared by customs, were available at the entry points visited; however, they do not contain all the information foreseen in Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 (amount allowed to be imported from specific countries). At present no further initiatives have been taken in order to increase public awareness as no information reflecting the provisions of the above Regulation is distributed to the passengers in aircraft or ships. There was no responsibility 4 defined to ensure that airline operators or shipping lines inform their passengers accordingly; it was stated that in-flight-announcements will be made in near future.

Organisation of controls/sanctions Passengers or vehicles from third countries are checked by customs according to the chosen red or green line/channel. At the green line/channel customs carries out randomised checks, which are part of normal customs surveillance and not specific to imports of live animals and products of animal origin. Checks on personal luggage are carried out on 1 -5 % of passengers per flight. Luggage is checked manually or ­ if available ­ with scanning equipment. There are no sniffer dogs trained for the detection of meat and milk products. Customs stated that the risk based approach to carry out these checks, is mainly based on the country of origin. Customs have no updated documentation available (e.g. list of third countries for fishery products) and they are not familiar with the use of this documentation. There are records (copies of the receipt of seized amount of products for the traveller) for cases of consignments seized; however, these records are not always completely filled in (e.g. no third country of origin, no weight). No summary record to give an overview for seized consignments in 2004 or number of controls per third country exists. For CITES-consignments the CCA provided an overview for the seized consignments of live animals and products of animal origin for the last three years (2002: 2 cases, 2003: 21 cases, 2004: 30 cases). Passengers are not liable for the cost of destruction of seized consignments or for any penalties laid down in Art. 4 of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004, if the illegal consignments are abandoned or seized after being discovered by customs. Customs believes that seizure of the relevant consignments is adequate sanction and they do not consider attempted illegal import of animal products as smuggling. There are also non-BIP-airport-entry-points for passengers with baggage arriving directly from third countries or from third countries through other EU airports (interline) and CCA stated that customs is present at the time of arrival of such flights. Specific findings for BIP-airport-entry point: - Flights from Asian countries have the highest priority regarding veterinary products. - As part of their integrated controls, customs scanned about 3 % of luggage from ca 10,000 passengers/day. 2/3 of the scanned consignments were opened and physically checked. The percentage of products of animal origin and live animals seized among these checks could not be clarified on the spot. - Seized consignments were collected in a fridge and every 2nd or 3rd month brought to the customs laboratory in Helsinki, which is responsible for the destruction (the method of destruction could not be clarified on the spot). Customs at the airport signed the delivery to the laboratory. No further records are kept. 5 - There were no amnesty bins for passengers voluntarily abandoning products of animal origin. Specific findings for BIP-road-entry point: - In 2004, 2,500,000 passengers passed the border, using 800,000 passenger cars, 450,000 trucks and 20,000 busses. About 50 % of the passengers entered from Russia, the other 50 % left Finland. - The vehicles can pass via the green line (passenger cars from EU or non- EU countries) or the red line (busses and passenger cars with something to declare). - From the vehicles passing the green line, randomised checks of 2 -5 % of the cars were carried out. - The busses with passengers from Russia and Finland were more often checked; 10 ­ 20 % of their luggage is scanned and in case of suspicion also opened. 5 ­ 10 % of the luggage of passengers of other nationalities was opened on the bus. - About 2 ­ 5 % of the truck drivers were checked. - There are no records for seized consignments for 2004 available. - The seized consignments in 2005 (about 100 kg meat products from Russia) were collected in a freezer under customs supervision. Each of the seized consignments was labelled with a record sheet and no further records were kept. The procedure for disposal and destruction of the consignments in accordance to Council Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002(h) has not been implemented at present. In 2004, seized products were given to truck drivers exiting to Russia. - A new record template has been developed in which instructions for disposal and destruction can be inserted. Specific findings for non-BIP-road-entry point: - About 10 passenger cars per day entered from Russia, which were all checked. Customs stated that, due to the checks already carried out by the Russian customs, there were no products of animal origin seized to date. 5.2.3. Import and transit of freight Although customs is responsible for identification and selection, the selection of the consignments subject to veterinary checks is not completely reliable and consignments may escape veterinary checks as both customs databases and the "handbook" used are not updated and not linked completely with the requirements for veterinary checks, as described in report 7646/2005. One consignment was stored 15 days at the port without veterinary checks performed. Specific findings for BIP-airport-entry point: - There are 150,000 t cargo freight per day, of which less than 1 % are physically checked. - Three out of fourteen staff of customs are responsible for opening consignments. - CA stated that no findings of illegal imported consignments were noted. 6 Specific findings for BIP-road-entry point: - In 2004, about 1,000,000 t freight consignments were imported, mainly timber and raw metal from Russia. - Each day about 450 trucks passed the border, 80 ­ 90 % of them are empty, about 40 ­ 50 trucks per day loaded with timber, 20 trucks per day loaded with container and 1 or 2 trucks have products to be veterinary checked by the BIP staff. Every truck is weighed, from the empty trucks 1 -2 % are scanned, and 50 % of the trucks with containers are checked by x-ray or opened. - 20 % of the traffic is transit traffic for which customs use the NTCS database. 80% are imports (including the TIR carnet procedure) for which the "ITU" database is used. Customs stated, that the procedure in "ITU" is opened after the veterinary checks at the BIP, because if the veterinary decision does not allow the consignment to be imported, it is difficult to finalise the procedure in "ITU". - No information was given that veterinary goods were detected but not declared as such. Specific findings for non-BIP-road-entry point: - For all incoming trucks from Russia 100 % documentary and identity checks and 10 % physical checks are carried out by customs. - There was no updated documentation available (e.g. no model health certificates, no third country list for fishery and milk products) and during the mission the access to the internet was not available.(4) - Customs stated that no illegal imports have been found to date. 5.2.4. Import of post consignments Customs are permanently present in the main point of entry for post which is also the main point of entry for express mail, packages or parcels; there are 38 other post offices where customs clearance of postal consignments is possible. Live animals cannot be sent by post under the "Postal Convention" but there are no general restrictions for foodstuff. In 2004, the main point of entry for post received 472,600 consignments (about 90% of all postal consignments to Finland). Randomised checks of about 1.5 % of these consignments were carried out. The main criteria to check express mail, packages or parcels is the value and consignments below 45 Euro are generally not opened as they are not taxed. Approximately 10 % of the consignments are taxed. The selection for consignments to be physically checked is based on its declared content and value, origin, destination and experience of the staff carrying out the risk assessment. There are no sniffer dogs, but a scanner is available. (4) In their response to the draft report the Finnish CCA noted that there was no updated documentation available as this information is provided via the internet pages of the MMM and during the mission the access to the internet was temporarily unavailable. 7 Each day, about 20 - 25 consignments were found not in line with legal requirements, approximately 15 of them containing food of animal origin. These consignments were marked by customs with a red label and stay at this postal office or will be delivered to one of the other 38 postal offices. The owner of the consignment can then choose whether to allow destruction or to provide a veterinary certificate to carry out the veterinary import control procedure. In case of seizure of food of animal origin from third countries the owner of the consignment signs a receipt (previous system, found in place on spot) and/or a declaration (new system, stated by CCA to be in place since 1.4.2005). The receipt contains basic information such as description of the seized food (e.g. "fish eggs"), amount, but not obligatory the weight, and the date of signature by the owner. Therefore there was no clear overview of the number of consignments of products of animal origin received by post as no records are kept from the outcome of the physical checks except of the copies of the receipts of the seizure. Customs does not use the customs database but the "handbook", as described in report 7646/2005. The CA stated that an updated version of the manual is in print. The positive list was present; however, customs was not familiar with the list. For destruction, seized consignments are sent under customs supervision to the Customs laboratory, which is responsible for destruction. No records regarding destruction were available at the mail office. 5.2.5. Import and transit of live animals An updated instruction for implementing the Regulation (EC) No 998/2003 was sent by VBI to customs, border guards, principal and municipal veterinary officer located at all points of entry. CCA stated that customs are equipped with readers for transponders at all relevant points of entry. At Vaalimaa road the CA stated that about 50 pet animals per month were checked by customs and that no training in addition to the annual one week training on restrictions, but sufficient information, was provided for this task. At Helsinki airport the CA stated that all pet animals arriving in cargo boxes are considered to be commercial and therefore are checked at the BIP. If customs have doubts whether non commercial pets fulfil the requirements for movements into or within the EU, the pets were temporarily housed in the facilities of the BIP.

recommendations.text: To ensure that follow-up controls carried out at LVUs are recorded in TRACES when required, for consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination, as provided for in Article 3(2)(c) of Decision 2004/292/EC and Article 48(3) of Regulation EC No 1069/2009.Recommendation based on conclusion 42. Associated findings 28-31, 34-35, 37 and 38.

citations.text: All of the re-imported goods via Finnish BIPs are indicated as channelled from the entry BIP to establishment of origin, as required. However, LVUs responsible do not always confirm in TRACES the arrival at destination (TRACES window 41 of the CVED is not filled in for most of them). BIPs staff stated that there is a written agreement of acceptance signed by the re-importer.

A number of consignments of blood products were imported, which require channelling (Annex XIV, Chapter II, Section 2 point 3.2 of Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011). About 50% of consignments were channelled in TRACES by the entry BIP, as required. Each of those consignments were confirmed by the LVU at destination using TRACES. The instructions for import controls did not cover the controls required for blood products, and the different officials interpreted the requirements of the Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 in different ways. The central competent authorities amended the instructions during the FVO audit and distributed these to the BIPs immediately.

Arrival of (rejected) consignments channelled to an incinerator for destruction was not confirmed in TRACES, contrary to the requirements. The reason is that the notification on the channelled consignment does not reach the environmental authority in charge of controls at the incinerator (who is not a TRACES user). It was noted that, instead of the TRACES confirmation, the system ensures that the BIP receives a paper document confirming the arrival at destination of the consignment. 5.2.8 Animal welfare checks

Some of the CVEDAs issued by BIPs in other Member States, with destination in controlled destinations in Finland, did not include records of the controls at destination in the control part of the TRACES document. 6 5.2.9 INTRA module

The INTRA documents for some consignments sent to control bodies in a different Member State, the "control part" had never been filled in by the authority at destination. One consignment of live animals exported via another Member States had no control part filled in at the point of exit from the EU. The authorities in Finland did not follow-up such cases to verify the reason for the absence of records in that control part.

A national instruction requires the filling in of the control part for documents of consignments of animals arriving for slaughter from other Member States. For other animals, all incoming consignments of live pigs and cattle should also be controlled at destination. However, there is only some evidence in TRACES of controls on such consignments having taken place. The missing information on the required controls did not trigger any action from the competent authority. The checks for other consignments are performed on the basis of risk or suspicion. 5.2.10 DOCOM module

Consignees are instructed to do checks on all consignments arriving from other Member States. If the place of destination is under the control of an official, the veterinarian should ensure that all the checks are done and record this in TRACES. 80% of DOCOMs arriving to Finland have the control part completed in TRACES. 74% of documents going out from Finland have the controls at destination recorded in TRACES.

Daily monitoring on the certificates provided in TRACES is carried out by EVIRA and regional official veterinarians. However, officials met at the LVUs were not always aware that some DOCOM notifications received via TRACES had not been followed up. Normally such notifications are deleted after a certain time, and the system does not ensure that notifications are followed up before being deleted. 7 5.2.11 CEDs and CHED-PPs modules

Finnish competent authorities are correctly using TRACES, with some specific exceptions (controls on consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination are not always recorded in the system). This lack of information in the system undermines the communication between competent authorities in relation to the specific controls. 5.3 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal requirements Regulation(EC) No 882/2004 Findings

audits.title: Organic production rules and the effectiveness of the control system

recommendations.text: Ensure that CtrlAs carry-out their controls in accordance with documented 2. procedures as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in particular that they implement the instructions issued by the CA. Ensure that when audits are performed, in order to verify the level of controls organised by the CtrlAs, appropriate measures are taken in the light of their results as required in Article 4 (6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 3. Ensure that information in any cases of irregularity or infringement affecting the organic status of a product shall be immediately communicated between the CtrlAs in accordance with Article 92(5) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and by the CtrlAs to the CA in accordance with Article 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 92(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 4. Ensure that information on the results of inspections and visits as referred to in Article 65 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 is communicated to the paying agency as required in Article 92(6) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 5. Ensure that risk assessment applied by CtrlAs serves as the basis to determine the nature and frequency of controls, as established in Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, and, in particular, that additional control visits are carried out on the basis of a general evaluation of the potential risk of a non-compliance, as established in Article 65 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 6. Ensure that additional random control visits are unannounced as required in Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 7. Ensure that the controls carried out by the CtrlAs are effective and appropriate, as required by Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in order for organic operators to comply with all the relevant requirements laid down in Regulations (EC) No 834/2007 and No 889/2008 and in particular as regards: the rules for the production of processed food as established in Article 26(4) and (5) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. the documentary accounts demonstrating the balance between inputs and outputs as established in Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, taking into account all relevant information, and the livestock records kept as required in Article 76(e) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, and the veterinary treatments in farms of animal husbandry as 23 required by Articles 24(4) and (5) and 76(e) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 8. Ensure that the control system as set up allows for the traceability of each product, at all stages of production, processing and distribution as required by Article 27(13) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and in line with Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. 9. Ensure that CtrlAs take and analyse samples for checking the conformity with organic production rules, in line with Article 65 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and in particular regarding the 5% minimum number of samples. 10. Ensure that checks on organic products originating from EU internal market (outside Finland) are not discriminatory as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 11. Ensure that requirements for the management of animals set out in Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 are complied with, in particular that dehorning is carried out only if authorised by the CA on a case-by-case basis. 12. Ensure that in cases of irregularities detected during official controls, the CtrlAs take appropriate measures without delay in order to ensure that products affected by these irregularities do not bear any reference to the organic production method as required in Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

recommendations.text: The CCA should ensure that CAs responsible for carrying-out internal audits have the 2. legal powers to take appropriate measures in the light of their results (Article 4 (6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2204) as required in Article 4(4) of Regulation (EC) No 3. 882/2004. 4. 5. The CCA shall ensure that when non-compliance are detected during official controls adequate actions (e.g. follow-up) are carried-out in order to ensure that FBOs remediate the situation as foreseen in Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The CA should ensure that a risk based approach is always used for the planning of controls as required in Article 3 (1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The CAs should ensure that any adaptation made by the CA to the procedures covering the presence of OVs in slaughterhouses is based on risk analysis as required in Paragraph 2, Chapter II, Section III, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and complies with the conditions set out in Point 2, Annex VIb to Regulation (EC) No 2074/2005 9. The CAs shall ensure that FBOs comply with the requirements laid down in Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 as required in Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, in particular that slaughterhouse and establishments under their responsibility meet the requirements laid down in Annex III, Sections II and V of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 10. The CA should ensure that controls over Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 include all relevant requirements of the Regulation and in particular the application of shelf-life studies for ready to eat products that can support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes. 11. In order to be designated, laboratories have to be accredited for pesticide residue analysis under ISO/IEC 17025, as required by Article 12 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Another criterion, taken into account by EVIRA for designation of laboratories, is the number of analytes sought. However, the scope of accreditation is not a criterion for designation. In addition, there are no clear instructions for designated laboratories with regard to methodology and implementation of laboratory analysis in order to detect and quantify substances not authorised for organic production, as required by Article 65 (2) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

In the first laboratory, a quality management system for routine pesticide residue analyses is in place. However, the audit team observed some weaknesses, including the following: 9 for standards, standard solutions and working solutions, records were available, but inconsistent labelling of standard solutions does not allow for a proper traceability; testing and replacement of standard solutions is performed by only a single injection and application of deviation criteria for comparison of old and new standards could not be demonstrated; requirements for identification and confirmations, i.e. application of acceptable deviations in retention time and ion ratio could not be demonstrated, which can result in false positive or false negative analytical results; for the analysis of organic samples, the corresponding quality control samples (routine recovery checks) are spiked at levels four times the reporting limit and underperformance of recovery data is not taken into account in reporting of results; this can have an impact on the quantification of pesticide residues; sample homogenisation is performed at room temperature, which is known to cause inadequate homogenisation, as well as degradation of certain analytes during sample preparation.

The overall performance of the second laboratory is generally good. Some weaknesses were identified in the implementation of routine pesticide residue analyses, such as: sample homogenization performed at room temperature, in-house validation data for some of the commodity groups was incomplete and traceability for calculation of analytical results could not be demonstrated comprehensively clear.

Laboratories for pesticide residue analysis in organic products have been designated. However, the lack of clear instructions from the CA for designated laboratories with regard to the methodology and implementation of laboratory analysis results in weaknesses in the implementation of routine pesticide residues analyses and may reduce the reliability of analytical results.

recommendations.text: To apply the risk-based approach in the development of the audit programme and ensure that the internal audits meet the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and cover all relevant areas of activity. Recommendation based on conclusion: 26. Associated findings: 22, 23, 24 and 25.

citations.text: The audit activities have consisted of one pilot project per year since 2014 and each project covers a specific area of the official controls. Plant health, the residue control programme for food of animal origin, and the Salmonella control programme are the three projects that have been carried out so far. In 2017, an audit project on the control of fertilisers will be carried out. The competent authority has prepared a multi-annual audit programme for the period 2015-2018 that includes areas based on the choices made by the Directors of Evira in the context of the pilot phase of the audit function. The purpose was to have audits in sectors that could be used for modelling and further developing the audit system. The topics mostly cover horizontal issues and are selected in such a way that 50 % are audit projects on food safety, 25 % on plant health and 25 % on animal health and welfare. 12

The audit programme is planned based on the resources available (capability of two audit projects per year) and it is considered that in five years there will be five projects on food safety and two or three projects on plant health and production and an equal number on animal health and welfare.

The audit system has not defined the audit universe and as regards the audit programme development, the process is not well-documented and transparent, and it does not include risk-based prioritisation.

The audit team noted that the extended scope and time-consuming nature of the audit programme and its execution combined with the limitations in the availability of human resources, makes it unfeasible to cover all relevant areas of official controls in a five- year period. Conclusions on the development of the programme of audits

The process for the audit programme development is not well-documented or transparent and it does not follow risk-based prioritisation, which means that it does not result in programmes that could achieve an appropriate risk-based coverage of relevant official control activities. The development of the audit programme is further constrained by the lack of stable and sufficient resources without which the continuity in the provision of audit services cannot be ensured. 5.2.5 Implementation of the audit process 5.2.5.1 Legal requirements Article 2(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states that "Audit" "means a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives." In section 5.1 of the Annex of Decision 2006/677/EC further guidance is provided to Member States on the `Systematic Approach', including: "A systematic approach should be applied to the planning, conduct, follow-up and management of audits. To that end, the audit process should: ....... -- be supported by documented audit procedures and records to ensure consistency between auditors and to demonstrate that a systematic approach is followed, -- include procedures for generating audit findings, including the identification of evidence of compliance and noncompliance, as appropriate, and for preparing, approving and distributing audit reports, -- include procedures to review audit conclusions, in order to identify system-wide strengths and weaknesses in the control system, disseminate best practice and ensure the monitoring of corrective and preventive actions, 13 -- be monitored and reviewed to ensure the audit programme's objectives have been met and to identify opportunities for improvement." Section 6.1 of the Annex of Commission Decision 2006/677 provides guidance on implementation of the Audit Process: "To comply with the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the audit system should cover the following three points set out in Article 2(6): (a) Verification of compliance with planned arrangements in order to provide assurances that official controls are carried out as intended and that any instructions or guidelines given to staff carrying out the controls are followed. This may largely be addressed by document review, but will also require on-site verification. The audit team will require good generic audit knowledge and skills to address this audit objective. (b) Verification of the effective implementation of planned arrangements. In order to assess effectiveness, that is the extent to which planned results are achieved, on-site operational implementation must be included. This should include an assessment of the quality and consistency of the controls and should involve on-site audit activities. The audit team will require the relevant technical expertise in order to address this audit objective. (c) The audit system should also seek to assess whether the planned arrangements are suitable to achieve the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and in particular the single integrated multi-annual national control plan. This should include assessing the suitability of official controls, with regard, for example, to their frequency and the methods applied, having regard to the structure of the production chain(s) and to production practices and volume. The audit team should have substantial knowledge and understanding of system auditing, together with relevant technical input to address this audit objective. In order to determine whether the planned arrangements are suitable to achieve the objectives set out in (c) above, the following should be considered: Audit criteria should include strategic objectives stemming from Regulations (EC) No 178/2002 and (EC) No 882/2004 (including the single integrated multi-annual national control plan) and national legislation. recommendations.text: To ensure that the competent authorities take appropriate measures in the light of the results of the internal audits carried out as required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 51. Associated findings: 49 and 50.

citations.text: The audit team noted that for the two audit projects that were carried out in in 2014 and 2015, the audited services have provided neither comments on the content of the draft 19 reports nor action plans to address the identified deficiencies (some of which were significant). The competent authority stated in the closing meeting that actions have been taken to address the recommendations of the audit reports but could not provide evidence at that time. By request of the DG SANTE audit team after the audit, the competent authority confirmed that no documented evidence related to the addressing of audit recommendations was available. Thus the competent authorities could not demonstrate that they take appropriate measures in the light of the results of the audits carried out, contrary to the requirement of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The audit team noted the lack of arrangements in place to ensure that issues are raised to the attention of the senior management so that the organisation takes responsibility and top management supports the audit function. This is in reference to longstanding deficiencies related to the results of the audits (delay in the finalisation of the reports because audited authorities do not provide comments on the draft reports in a timely manner (or at all), lack of corrective action plans etc.). Conclusions on follow-up of audit recommendations

The competent authority does not ensure that audit results are acted upon therefore the impact of the audit function on the quality and the effectiveness of official controls is limited. The need to implement corrective actions in response to audit results is not brought to the attention and ownership of senior management and thereby deficiencies in the performance of the official controls can remain outstanding/reoccur for a long period of time. 5.2.7 Transparency 5.2.7.1 Legal requirements Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires, inter alia, that "audits ........shall be carried out in a transparent manner". Section 5.2 of the Annex of Commission decision 2006/677 provides guidance on transparency, including the following: "In order to demonstrate the audit process is transparent, documented procedures should, in particular, include a clearly defined audit planning process, audit criteria and audit report approval and distribution mechanisms. Management and implementation of the audit process should be transparent to all relevant stakeholders. In particular, there should be full transparency between the audit body and the auditee. Ensuring the audit process is transparent in the eyes of other stakeholders will assist in the dissemination of information, and in particular in the sharing of best practice within and between competent authorities. 20 The Member States should adopt the appropriate measures to ensure their audit systems are transparent, taking national legal and other requirements into account. To that end, the Member States should consider encouraging practices that improve the transparency of the process." 5.2.7.2 Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that sample checks and testing (qualitative and quantitative), as appropriate, are carried in food produced in Finland as well as in GMO containing feed, as required by Article 9.1 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003, in order to ensure compliance with this Regulation. Recommendation based on conclusions No 29 and 30. Associated findings No 24, 25 and 26.

citations.text: Evira informed the audit team that it does not consider surveillance of national production through sampling and testing necessary, because the Customs' checks on incoming food ingredients (used by domestic producers) is considered to provide sufficient safeguards since GMOs are not commercially grown in Finland. According to Evira no food items containing GMOs are produced in Finland and consequently as the customs already checks the imported potential GM ingredients, there is little need to check potential cross contamination again at the national production level. Annual tests carried out up to 2013 did not, according to Evira, give any non-compliant test results. However, due to the subsequent absence of any level of sampling and testing, coupled with the limited knowledge of the total population of operators that handle ingredients relevant to GMOs by Evira (see paragraph 44), the latter is not in a position to demonstrate that documentary checks are effective.

Evira classifies feed business operators into risk categories. The classification determines the frequency of inspection. Production of medicated feed, use of animal proteins and production volume are the main factors determining the risk category. As regards GMOs, Evira has chosen to almost exclusively sample and test (for authorised and non-EU-authorised GMOs) feed that is not labelled as containing GMOs (not supposed to contain authorised GMOs above a 0.9% level). However, there is no evidence that feed containing authorised GMO above 0.9% (and labelled as such) is less 7 likely to contain non-EU-authorised GMOs supporting its exclusion from sampling and testing.

Concerning paragraphs 24 and 25, Article 9.1 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003 requires Member States to ensure that inspections and other control measures including sample checks and testing (qualitative and quantitative), as appropriate, are carried out to ensure compliance with the Regulation while Article 4.2(a) of Regulation (EU) No 882/2004 requires CAs to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls.
However, the effectiveness of documentary checks at Finnish food business operators is not underpinned with surveillance through sampling and testing of nationally produced food.

With regard to feed, excluding GMO containing feed from testing for non-EU- authorised GM events has the potential to reduce the effectiveness of the official controls. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Controls of the authorised deliberate release of GMOs Legal requirements Articles 4(1), 4(3), 4(5), 6, 8, 9, 10 and 31(3) of Directive 2001/18/EC. recommendations.text: To include all EU requirements on Food Improvement Agents in the scope of official controls, in order to ensure their effectiveness as required by Article 4.2a of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 43

citations.text: There is a system in place for the official controls of FIAs, including import, marketing and their use that is overall fit for purpose, and includes appropriate action in case of non-compliance. However, not all requirements of the EU legislation on FIAs are presently included in the controls and therefore not subject to verification and enforcement, as appropriate. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The system of official food controls related to production, trade and use of Food Improvement Agents currently in place can largely verify effectively that their use is in line with the applicable EU legislation. This system was found to be implemented as foreseen, in practice. Control personnel are supported by dedicated staff at central level to provide the necessary technical assistance. In addition, publicly available guidelines and the peer control network of the competent authorities on FIAs provide additional support aimed at achieving compliance with the legal requirements. However, certain elements of the applicable EU legislation are presently not covered by the official controls, thus preventing enforcement where so required. 5 https://ec.europa.eu/food/sites/food/files/safety/docs/fs_food-improvement-agents_guidance_1333- 2008_annex-2.pdf 10 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 14 June with representatives of Evira. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. The CAs made no comments on the findings and conclusions, but stressed that the challenges should be addressed at EU level. 8 RECOMMENDATION No. Recommendation 1. recommendations.text: To ensure that the checks of consignments of food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions are performed in line with Articles 8(1)(a) and 8(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009, Articles 9(1) and 9(2) of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014, Articles 8(1) and 8(2) of Regulation (EU) No 2015/175 and Articles 10(1) of Regulation (EU) No 2016/6 at the designated points of entry, designated points of import or control points which meet the requirements laid down in Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 and Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014 as appropriate. Recommendation based on conclusions: 61 and 71 Associated findings: 38, 39, 40 and 63

citations.text: The documentary checks of food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions are carried out at the Customs Electronic Centre (at central level) and not in the listed DPEs. The listed DPEs are "virtual" with neither physical facilities nor personnel available on-the-spot to perform the documentary checks. This procedure is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 8(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009, Article 9(1) of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014, Article 8(1) of Regulation (EU) No 2015/175 and Article 10(1) of Regulation (EU) No 2016/6.

The operators comply with the obligation to pre-notify the arrival of their consignments: those that use TRACES e-mail scanned copies of the Common Entry Documents (CEDs) to Customs, and where required, scans of the certificates, declarations, laboratory test results and other required documentation, e.g. invoices, prior to the physical arrival of the goods. Customs verify the scanned documents but never request originals of the certificates or laboratory result reports. This hinders the verification of the authenticity of the health certificates, declarations and the laboratory results due to the reliance on scanned documents, which is contrary to the requirements of Article 5 and 9(2) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 884/2014, Article 5 and 8 of Regulation (EU) 2015/175 and Article 5 and 10 of Regulation (EU) No 2016/6.

The listed DPEs have no facilities for carrying out identity and physical checks. The identity and physical checks are performed upon request of the Customs Electronic Centre at the Customs' authorised warehouses by trained Customs staff.

The way in which the system for documentary checks of the consignments of food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions has been set up (checks are being carried out centrally instead of at the entry points at the border) is contrary to EU requirements. Furthermore, Customs do not check the originals of certificates or other relevant documents and therefore are not in a position to ascertain their authenticity.

The seven listed DPEs have no dedicated facilities for carrying out the import checks (documentary, identity and physical checks, including sampling). The identity and physical checks are performed upon request of the Customs Electronic Centre at the Customs' authorised warehouses (for details, see section 5.2.4.3) and no list is available of DPIs and control points. Contrary to the requirement of Article 8 of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Article 19(2) of Regulation (EC) 669/2009, Customs has not published a list of DPIs and control points as the goods must be inspected in Customs authorised warehouses. Information on the warehouses can be obtained through the warehouse search at the following website: https://tulli.fi/en/e-services/search-and-query- services/warehouse-ids. 5.4.2 BIP Vaalimaa

The authorities have not put in place appropriate physical facilities within the listed DPEs, and there is no list of DPIs and control points available. The system in place does not satisfy the EU requirement that documentary checks should be performed at the border and cannot ensure that checks on consignments of products of non-animal origin subject to special import controls are carried out under the suitable and hygienic conditions expected of DPEs and DPIs. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authorities have set up an adequate framework for carrying out official controls on animals and products of animal origin intended for import into the EU. This framework is supported by good cooperation based on regular meetings and interactive communication between the Finnish Food Authority and Customs. The competent authorities 15 have put suitable arrangements in place to ensure staff are trained and are kept up-to-date in their area of competence. There is a monitoring plan in place which aims to support officials in identifying relevant consignments of goods for testing. The administrative framework, therefore, contributes to ensuring that the official import controls are largely carried out to a consistent standard. The implementation of import controls of animals and products of animal origin was generally in line with EU requirement and could ensure that only compliant consignments are introduced into the territory of the EU. Appropriate measures were undertaken for the rejected and re-imported consignments. However, the same could not be said about the implementation of checks on products of non- animal origin subject to special import conditions. The way in which the system for documentary checks of these consignments has been set up is contrary to EU requirements. While the competent authority has designated seven points of entry for products subject to special import conditions, there are no dedicated facilities at these points and all the documentary checks are carried out centrally (and not at the border as required by EU law). Furthermore, during the documentary checks, the competent authority only verifies the e- mailed scanned copies of the certificates or other required documents and not their originals. By doing so the competent authority is not in a position to ascertain the authenticity of presented documents. Controls on travellers' personal luggage, postal parcels and returning empty livestock vehicles contribute to preventing the introduction and spread of African swine fever and other animal diseases in the EU. The facilities and equipment of the two visited BIPs, including the new ones at the BIP Helsinki airport were adequate for the official controls of the animals and goods within their approval categories. However, the points of entry and import and control points for the import controls of products of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions are not designated in line with relevant EU requirements and thus cannot provide the guarantees as to the suitability and hygiene conditions applicable. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 21 May 2019 with the representatives of the central authorities of the FFA and Customs. At this meeting, the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. The central competent authorities did not express disagreement with the findings and conclusions presented. 16 8 RECOMMENDATIONS No. Recommendation 1. To ensure that the checks of consignments of food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions are performed in line with Articles 8(1)(a) and 8(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009, Articles 9(1) and 9(2) of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014, Articles 8(1) and 8(2) of Regulation (EU) No 2015/175 and Articles 10(1) of Regulation (EU) No 2016/6 at the designated points of entry, designated points of import or control points which meet the requirements laid down in Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 a

recommendations.text: To ensure that inspections of feed manufacturers are carried out without the systematic issuing of prior notice to operators, except where such notice is necessary and duly justified, as required by Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion: 28. Associated finding: 18.

citations.text: The audit team noted that operational instruction 12729/8 requires that "inspections must be carried out unannounced unless a notification is necessary and justified shortly before the inspections to ensure the presence of the staff and documents required for the inspection". However, the FFA informed the audit team that, in case of inspections of feed manufacturers (i.e. manufacturers of feed materials, feed additives/premixtures and compound feed), 5 between two and four weeks notice is normally given to the operators. The FFA stated that such a notice period is necessary for inspectors to be adequately prepared and allows for the request and analysis of relevant documents in advance. The audit team scrutinised three cases selected at random. In all, the time between the original notification of the operator and the date when the requested documentation was supposed to be provided by the operator was substantial ­ from one and a half to five weeks. The information provided by the FFA did not demonstrate that there had been any audit-related preparatory work in this period. The audit team pointed out that while prior notice can be justified in rare cases (remote locations, irregular working hours, etc.), systematic provision of prior notice is not in line with the requirements laid down by Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The FFA further specified that the control activities carried out on the only group of FeBOs systematically announced in advance (i.e. feed manufacturers) comprised 15% of all types of the control activities.

The inspection planning system is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out on all operators regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. However, the effectiveness of the system is weakened by providing unjustified prior notice of inspections to feed manufacturers, shortcomings in the assessment of operators' HACCP plans, and incomplete verification of the appropriateness of operators' retained samples. citations.text: For the establishments listed in section 2 of this report, the audit team scrutinised the inspectors' assessments of operators' HACCP plans, analysed the most recent reports of the official controls performed and interviewed the inspectors involved. recommendations.text: To put in place mechanisms to ensure that the central competent authority has oversight to verify the effectiveness, appropriateness, and consistency of the official controls on dairy establishments and milk production holdings as required by Article 5.1 (a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and to ensure adequate coordination and collection of information between the competent authorities involved in the controls, in order to enable coordinated implementation of the multi-annual control plan, and its review, as required by Article 109 of Regulation (EU) 2017/. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 34 and 35. Associated findings Nos 19, 29, and 32.

citations.text: The Finnish constitution enables the local CAs, which are the main implementing authorities with regard to food safety, to operate with very substantial autonomy. According to Article 32 of the Food Act they must carry out food controls within their territory as provided for in the Act and submit notifications and reports to the regional CAs and CCA in accordance with the food regulations. Furthermore, they are to advise FBOs and consumers and provide information on matters covered by the Food Act.

Although evidence of flows of information from top-down and vice versa between the central, regional and local CAs was provided to the audit team, the change of IT tools has resulted in gaps of information flows (see paragraph 32). At the time of the audit the FA had crude data available on the official controls carried out at national level and the percentage of performance (Oivahymy) scores given during dairy inspections. However, they had no real-time information readily available on the planned official controls and sampling of the local CAs that could be used for national planning of the official controls.

The CAs involved in food safety and veterinary controls use several IT tools for data input and to support planning and analysis of different activities and new information systems have been developed in recent years. At the time of the audit the new IT system VATI (keskitetty valvontatietojärjestelmä) had been introduced. The central, regional and local CAs have, dependent on the IT tool, different access rights: KUTI (kunnallinen tietojärjestelmä) was used in 2013-2018 to enable the regional and central CAs to collect and browse information on controls of establishments and holdings (on holdings only since 2016) from three different IT tools used by different municipalities. The CAs do still have viewing access to it. The audit team could verify that the local CAs interviewed had used their own IT tools. VATI replaced KUTI in January 2019. The local CAs feed data of their planned and implemented annual controls on FBOs into VATI. VATI contains basic information on types of controls carried out (documentary check or inspection), types of inspections carried out (e.g. pre-approval, planned, or follow-up inspections), their duration and costs (chargeable or free of charge), action(s) in case of non- compliance(s) (guidance, request for action or administrative/coercive measures, reason for non-compliance). The audit team noted the following: i. The CCA stated that all local CAs have started to use VATI and that the system will be developed further. ii. The local CAs are supposed to upload the planned official controls, sampling and analyses, diagnostic tests on dairy holding and establishments and the results thereof into VATI. This information should be accessible to all levels of CAs. However, this was not yet the case at the time of the audit as the CCA and regional CAs have no access to the planned controls and official sampling of the local CAs in VATI and if they want to check this, they need to consult the local CAs. The CCA stated that was because all reporting bases were not yet available during the audit. 9 iii. Upcoming inspections of FBOs, based on the inspection frequency that VATI calculates automatically depending on risk criteria, are flagged in VATI. However, if the CA wants to know if it is time to check certain topics (for example, HACCP-based procedures, that need to be checked once in a three year period) this has to be checked case by case going through the previous reports. iv. The local CA can change the inspection frequency given by VATI, but has to put in a justification into the IT tool. v. The central and regional CAs were not able to filter data according to certain parameters, unlike what they could do in KUTI (for example. holdings with direct sale of raw milk could be filtered)2. vi. The CAs met from one region stated that they would not be able to extract individual reports from VATI3. vii. The national guidance for officials on notification of incidences where residues of antibiotics are detected and reported by the FBO lacks details about how these incidents should be recorded in VATI. Some of the OVs met stated they would do this and some said they would not. In one region, the regional CA stated this information is available only in local CAs. viii. Some of the local CAs interviewed stated that they had not received sufficient training on the use of VATI. ix. During the migration of dairy holding data from KUTI to VATI, some data was duplicated and not all data have been checked for correctness4. VYHA (ympäristöterveydenhuollon valvontayksikkötietojen hallintajärjestelmä) is an IT tool used for registering data on resources and controls (which are part of the multiannual national control plan, VASU,) of the regional and local CAs. VYHA is run under the MHSA. The CAs have to input results of the previous year's control activities, including controls of tobacco, food safety, veterinary activities, consumer protections and health protection. The results have to be in by 31 March. The FA extract

The constitutional structure of Finland allows the local CAs to operate with very substantial autonomy. The central and regional CAs have no enforcement powers over the local CAs in relation to controls on dairy hygiene and the CCA have very limited oversight to verify the effectiveness, consistency and uniformity of the official controls.

At the time of the audit, the central and regional CAs had restricted access to the main control database VATI intended to support the controls system. Limited training has been organised for the local CAs on its use. The official controls are further hampered by the complexity, and difficulties in use, of IT applications and databases and problems related to transfer of dairy holding control data from old databases, which impairs the reliability of the data5.

citations.text: The FA was not able to provide an overview of the situation regarding the controls planned on dairy holdings in 2018-2020, even if the local CAs had entered the information into VATI. At national level, the annual target of inspecting 20 % of dairy holdings was not reached in 2018-2020. For example, one of the regional CAs interviewed reported that 10% of the dairy holdings were inspected in 2019.

In the regions examined by the audit team, some local CAs had not reached their annual inspection targets for dairy holdings and some local CAs had not carried out any inspections within a year. For example, one local CA that had 67 dairy holdings in the control area had set the annual target to 13 inspections annually. The authorities had carried out 13 inspections in 2019, none in 2020 and so far 6 in 2021. Another local CA that had 61 dairy holdings in their control plan had checked 2 holdings in 2018, 4 14 holdings in 2019, 7 in 2020 and so far 3 in 2021 (9 more holdings planned for 2021 which were last inspected in 2013).

The official controls on dairy hygiene cover the topics listed in the CCA's guidelines. Based on the reports seen and discussions with the inspectors the grading of shortcomings and the use of emoticons is not strictly in line with the guidelines - a more lenient approach is followed. The system is further weakened by not reaching the annual inspection targets and by the fact that the results in VATI are not necessarily reliable.

citations.text: Besides the official controls, milk co-operatives belonging to the dairy plants provide guidance and services to dairy holdings. The milk co-operative's inspectors write reports of their visits. The audit team was provided with a copy of one such report. The report was very detailed and included recommendations and actions to take, including deadlines. However, no follow- up inspection took place although there were serious shortcomings (including animal welfare ones to be corrected immediately) and the FBO had not informed the local CA of the situation (see paragraph 79) although Article 14 of the Animal Welfare Law 4.4.1996/247 requires to either help an animal that is injured, sick or helpless or to notify the CAs.

The CCA responsible for the official controls over the dairy sector stated that the co- operation between the milk co-operatives and CAs varies, depending on the individuals and stated that these entities should be included in the official controls (these entities are also responsible for the collection and transport of raw milk, see paragraph 79). 5.4.1 Health requirements for raw milk and colostrum

The dairy co-operatives responsible for the collection and transport of raw milk are not included in official controls and their co-operation with the CAs is not always adequate. 5.5 CONTROLS ON RAW MILK UPON COLLECTION Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. The collection and transport of raw milk from the dairy holdings to the dairy establishments is organised by milk co-operatives belonging to the dairy plants. The FBOs buy the milk from the farmers, organise the milk collections (usually every second day) and provide them with milk collection tanks. These organisations are not covered by the official controls (see paragraphs 58 and 59). The audit team examined one dairy holding report of a consultant a milk collection co-operative. recommendations.text: To ensure that areas are categorised as `remote' only when they fulfil the criteria of Union legislation, following the required risk assessment. Legal basis: Article 3.23, Article 19.1(b) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, Point d of Section 2 of Chapter III of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. Recommendation based on conclusion: 16. Associated findings: 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 3.23, Article 19.1(b) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, Point d of Section 2 of Chapter III of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. Recommendation based on conclusion: 16. Associated findings: 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15.

citations.text: Domestic legislation defines the areas that have been categorised as `remote' under Article 19(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. For ABP derived from some species, the entire territory of Finland is considered a remote area. In particular, ABP from slaughtering of horses and from aquatic animals can be disposed of by burial or landfilling throughout Finland, when authorised under environmental rules. However, according to the FFA, operators do not routinely avail of these possibilities.

This was confirmed during interviews held in a region where fish processing is an important economic activity. The audit team noted that, while this area was categorised as `remote' for ABP from aquatic animals, there were arrangements in place for collection and use of such ABP, in particular for feeding to fur animals or for other purposes outside the feed chain. Some of the inspection reports of food operators processing fish in other parts of Finland indicated similar collection arrangements for ABP.

The audit team noted that slaughtering of horses usually takes place in multi-species slaughterhouses, the majority of which are located in areas where ABP of the other species slaughtered are collected. ABP from horses can therefore be collected from such slaughterhouses. This was confirmed during the interview of an official veterinarian, who was substituting for other official veterinarians in several slaughterhouses, some of which were slaughtering horses.

Based on the above-mentioned, the audit team noted that there are viable collection and transport arrangements in areas that have been categorised as `remote' and consequently such areas do not meet the definition of a `remote area', as laid down in Article 3(23) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

FFA representatives stated that for those species for which the entire territory of Finland is categorised as a `remote area', the risk assessments referred to in point (d) of Section 2 of Chapter III of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 were not carried out. 5 Conclusion on the system in place for collection, use and disposal on ABP and DP

The system in place for collection, use and disposal of ABP and DP is largely adequate. For ABP derived from some species (fish, horses), the entire territory of Finland has been defined as a `remote area'. However, such designation is not justified since operational means of collection, disposal and use of ABP are available throughout the entire country. In practice, despite the absence of a risk assessment carried out by the competent authority, the impact of this shortcoming is probably limited and the quantities of ABP that might be disposed of by burial or landfilling are likely to be small, as most operators seem to make use of the existing collection arrangements. 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ALONG THE ABP CHAIN 5.3.1 Registration, approval and listing of ABP plants, establishments and operators

recommendations.text: To ensure that intra-species recycling of fur animals only takes place in farms registered by the competent authority for that purpose. Legal basis: Point 3(a)(i) of Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 Recommendation based on conclusion: 27. Associated finding: 21, 22, 23, 24, 25 and 26.
recommendations.legal_basis: Point 3(a)(i) of Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 Recommendation based on conclusion: 27. Associated finding: 21, 22, 23, 24, 25 and 26.

citations.text: The FFA has implemented a system for registration of fur animal farms where the feeding of fur animals (foxes and racoon dogs) with proteins derived from animal of the same species can take place (such feeding is hereafter referred to as `intra-species recycling'). An accurate and complete registration of farm is important for the purpose of official controls, as operators must comply with specific requirements (Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011). Farms where intra-species recycling take place are registered in the animal keepers' register with an indication of the concerned species (for other farms there is a statement that intra-species recycling is not carried out). 6

The FFA, despite efforts to spread the information to fur animal farmers, noted that around 50% of all fur animal farms are currently registered for intra-species recycling, which is believed to be far below the percentage of farms actually involved in intra- species recycling. This incomplete registration was confirmed during the interview of RVO of a region where most of the fur animals are located.

The audit team noted that inspections of fur animal farms must verify that these are correctly registered for intra-species recycling, if applicable. However, some MVO interviewed stated that they usually rely on the farmers statement that they are registered (or not) rather than checking the register. This led to situations where, when comparing register information and the corresponding inspection reports, the audit team noted contradictory information.

The audit team also noted that the information contained in the register was not fully reliable. The FFA explained that the migration of data between the previous and current IT system supporting the animal keepers' register resulted in inconsistencies in the information recorded. The FFA stated that the data contained in the register would be corrected.

RVO carry out checks on animal welfare, including at fur farms, during which is it required that the information contained in the animal keepers' register is checked (in general and not only for intra-species recycling). Some RVO interviewed stated that during such checks, in case of incorrect registration, the farmer is asked to update the register and that this is usually done orally. As a consequence, the FFA could not provide evidence of such checks or that follow-up had taken place in case of incorrect registration (which, in any case, would prove difficult in the absence of official records).

Based on the above-mentioned gaps, the ability of the current system to ensure that the register of fur animal farms (where intra-species recycling occurs) is updated over time is rather limited and this register is likely to remain incomplete. This does not ensure that the requirements of point 3(a)(i) of Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 are fulfilled. Conclusion on registration, approval and listing

Arrangements in place for registration, approval and listing provide assurance that the vast majority of operators active along the chain of ABP and DP are known, which facilitates the implementation of official controls. However, an incomplete and, currently, not reliable registration of fur farms concerned with intra-species recycling prevents the system from being fully in line with Union rules. 5.3.2 Planning of official controls
