citations.text: The audit team noted that official controls carried out by MVO cover burial of ABP in remote areas. FFA has issued guidance on burial, which encompasses all relevant requirements of Union legislation. However, such guidance does not specify how municipal veterinarians can verify that burial of ABP does not result in risks to underground water, as required by point 3(b) of Section 1 of Chapter III of Annex VI to 9 Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. In addition, MVO involved in inspections on disposal of bovine animals in a remote area, confirmed to the audit team that burial conditions were not checked during official controls, in particular whether burial locations were chosen to minimise risks to underground water. This does not fulfil the requirements of Section 3 of Chapter III of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

Official controls are mostly implemented as planned and are largely suitable to assess the applicable Union requirements on ABP and DP. There are, however, exceptions such as verification of burial conditions in remote areas, where such controls do not cover all applicable requirements. This might result in potential risks to water from burial of ABP in these areas. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Official controls are largely adequate to verify compliance with Union requirements on ABP and DP. These controls are well documented and operators along the entire chain of ABP are subject to regular checks. There are, however, some shortcomings in controls on burial conditions of fallen stock in `remote areas' (which do not verify the absence of risks to underground water), and the registry of fur farms where intra-species recycling may take place has not been completed, resulting in a lack of reliable information on such farms. For ABP derived from some species (fish, horses), the entire territory of Finland has been defined as a `remote area'. However, such designation is not justified since operational means of collection, disposal and use of ABP are available throughout the entire country. In practice, despite the absence of a risk assessment carried out by the competent authority, the impact of this shortcoming is probably limited and the quantities of ABP that might be disposed of by burial or landfilling are likely to be small, as most operators seem to make use of the existing collection arrangements. 11 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting took place by videoconference on 20 April 2021 with the FFA representatives. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. The competent authority representatives did not express disagreement with these. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authority is requested to provide details of the actions taken and planned aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, including deadlines for their completion, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. citations.text: Senior Meat Inspection Unit officers carry out approximately six `assessment and guidance' visits to slaughterhouses annually, where meat inspection arrangements and controls by OVs are checked and assessed. Normally, two of these visits take place in large establishments, the rest in low-capacity ones. The Animal Welfare and Identification Unit also carries out control visits to slaughterhouses. Regional managers' visits focus on staff support and HR-style aspects but also on mentoring and advising staff on meat inspection and official controls matters.

Taking into account the number of approved establishments and the frequency of visits, large slaughterhouses should receive an `assessment and guidance' visit every seven or eight years, and a low-capacity establishment once every ten or eleven years.(2)

The system to prioritise slaughterhouses to be visited by senior officers considers aspects like issues identified by OVs and enforcement taken. Establishments where OVs identify no or very few non-compliances are given low priority.

There are no regular checks at central level in order to establish if the OVs in approved slaughterhouses have a system in place to ensure that all the required controls are carried out within the agreed three-year cycle. In all establishments reviewed by the audit team, there were some controls that had not been completed at all during the last three years. Examples included `compliance with requirements of approval' or `vermin control'.

Although the CA provided some good examples of suitable and timely enforcement that had achieved positive outcomes, the audit team observed several examples where non- compliances were not identified or inadequate rating was given to those non- compliances that had actually been found. As lower rating non-compliance do not require the FBO to produce an action plan to resolve them or the OV to follow them up, an inadequately rated non-compliance has an impact on the likelihood of it being satisfactorily resolved.

Equally, there was also evidence of lack of follow up actions by OVs in some instances that the rating of a non-compliance required it, to ensure the FBO remedied the identified problems and/ or prevented the recurrence of the problem. (3) In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that Regional Directors or Senior inspectors of the Meat Inspection Unit contact official veterinarians if no reports have been submitted. (4) In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that the Animal Welfare and Identification Unit monitors the annual inspections and request missing reports. It also uses the annual reports to identify any deviations and provides feedback on the findings and guidance on actions to be taken to the relevant OVs. There are instructions in relation to the content of the annual animal welfare inspection 9

The design and implementation of the official control system does not provide assurance that controls over EU requirements and their enforcement are carried out correctly and uniformly across the 15 large and 44 low-capacity slaughterhouses. The system does not ensure that controls in respect of general hygiene requirements and welfare during slaughter actually take place with an appropriate frequency, or at all.

There are shortcomings in the identification, rating, action taken and follow-up of enforcement of non-compliances by the establishment OVs and in the CA supervision of those OVs that weaken the effectiveness of the enforcement that takes place.

In low-capacity slaughterhouses, FFA guides OVs to carry out hygiene monitoring activities 6-20 hours a year. If the low-capacity slaughterhouse operates less than once a month, the monitoring activities can be reduced by 50%. In reality, and as explained by the OVs dealing with low-capacity establishments, due to time constraints and clashes with their other professional activities, they do not spend any substantial amount of time to observe and assess FBOs' compliance with hygiene requirements during slaughter operations. The OVs in the low-capacity slaughterhouses visited did not routinely spend time observing the slaughter operations. As OVs, their time is usually dedicated exclusively to AMI and PMI. Only during the OIVA inspection, they might spend some time observing the slaughter operations, but not in all cases.

The time dedicated to official controls by OVs in low-capacity slaughterhouses, other than to carry out AMI and PMI, is very limited and affects the OVs' capacity to observe and assess the slaughterhouse hygiene practices and take necessary enforcement action where and when required.

In response to these findings the MFCAs reaction indicated that the lack of resources was a justification for some of them, and that some of the controls had not been recorded in the VATI system. citations.text: According to the information provided by FFA and MFCAs, fishing vessels are not controlled within the set frequencies. Despite being included at national level in the Finnish MANCP, the audit team did not find evidence in the relevant MFCAs that their control plans follow the MANCP and include controls of fishing vessels (food safety requirements). From the 56 vessels (see section 4.2 above), in 2019, 11 fishing vessels (over 12 metres) were controlled, 14 in 2020, and 6 in 2021. Moreover, the current approach for vessels under 12 metres is not in accordance with the requirements set out in Article 67 (b) of Regulation (EU) No 2019/627.

The audit team visited a primary production fishing vessel (cooled sea water) and found it broadly compliant with the applicable rules, except for the temperature requirements set in the operational (self-control) manual for the vessel which stated that fish loaded on board and maintained in cooled sea water, should be kept at not more than 5°C. This is not in line with the requirements set in Point I(B)(3) of Chapter I of Section VIII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 (not more than 3°C 6 hours after loading and not more than 0°C 16 hours after loading). According to the operator, the last control of the vessel was in 2018, however no records of that visit were available.

recommendations.text: The FFA should ensure that official controls of fishery products include the organoleptic examinations required in Article 70(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/62, and are carried out as required in Chapter(I)(A) and (C) of Annex VI to the same Regulation ­ "Random organoleptic controls" and "Random testing for histamine". Recommendation based on conclusion No 101. Associated finding No 84 and 87 to 92.

citations.text: With regard to organoleptic examinations, the audit team noted that the MCFAs visited do not perform them, despite it being clearly requested in the FFA guidance that such examinations be carried out. FFA indicated that staff from ELY carries out some organoleptic examinations during the landing controls, however incidental records of those controls are not made available to the food control authorities. The audit team also noted that the FFA guidance document provides for generic descriptions of organoleptic characteristics as standards and not Regulation (EC) 2406/96 as indicated in Chapter I(A) of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

Specifically for histamine, the FFA guidance indicates that "sampling for histamine shall be included in official controls, unless the activity is very small and the operator can demonstrate that self-monitoring is adequate". Additionally, for imported products tested at the EU border, it indicates that official sampling is not required.

The official controls carried out by the MCFAs do not include all the relevant provisions set out in Chapter I of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Organoleptic examinations, random testing for histamine and risk-based parasite testing are not carried out as required. The latter is due to an incorrect translation of the Finnish version of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. 5.4 FOLLOW UP OF IRASFF NOTIFICATIONS Legal requirements Articles 50(5) and 52 of Section 1 Chapter IV to Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council. citations.text: In addition, the possibility of using laboratories not designated by the authority(ies) does not comply with the above requirements above. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The official control system in place is clearly organised and supported by extensive and detailed written instructions/guidance. However, its operation is hindered notably by shortcomings concerning the adherence to the planned inspection frequency, which according to the MFCAs are linked to limited personnel resources, and the assessment and grading of deficiencies that often results in an overly positive evaluation of the shortcomings identified during the official controls. The control system does not cover primary production fishing vessels and aquaculture farms and the official controls covering the products do not fully respect the applicable requirements for histamine testing and organoleptic examinations. Additionally, some guidance provided to the control authorities and operators diverges from the current EU rules in different subjects such as operations associated with primary production and temperature requirements for certain vessels. The above impacts on the ability for the competent authorities to verify and enforce effectively the correct implementation of relevant EU requirements. 24 7 CLOSING MEETING During the closing meeting held by videoconference on 25 March 2022, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit to the competent authorities. citations.text: The staff interviewed by the audit team were largely familiar with the sampling instructions. However, the audit team noted three cases (all in slaughterhouses) where either only random sampling was carried out or the decision on the carcasses to sample was solely made on the basis of a documentary check without seeing/checking the animals/carcasses. This approach is not fully in line with pertinent legal requirements (11).

Whilst the residue monitoring plan is generally implemented promptly and in full in accordance with planned arrangements and in line with EU rules, some shortcomings in sample targeting in slaughterhouses allied with a failure to ensure the integrity of the chain of custody of the samples taken in slaughterhouses (pending their dispatch to the laboratory), have the potential to compromise the effectiveness of the plan. 5.4. citations.text: Interviewed officials indicated that, pending dispatch to the laboratory, the samples could be stored in refrigerators, freezers or at ambient temperature (e.g. honey), depending on the matrix and the analyte concerned. The audit team noted that, in the slaughterhouses, the samples were normally stored unsealed in the operator's equipment (refrigerator or freezer) during up to one week with unrestricted access to the equipment by the operator's staff. Such a practice does not ensure that the chain of custody is sufficiently maintained, and is not fully in line with pertinent legal requirements (15).

Whilst the residue monitoring plan is generally implemented promptly and in full in accordance with planned arrangements and in line with EU rules, some shortcomings in sample targeting in slaughterhouses allied with a failure to ensure the integrity of the chain of custody of the samples taken in slaughterhouses (pending their dispatch to the laboratory), have the potential to compromise the effectiveness of the plan. 5.4. citations.text: In the regions visited, the audit team scrutinised 11 non-compliant results, including the follow-up actions, identified in 2019-2021 and observed the following: a. sample submission to the laboratory, completion of analyses and reporting of test results were generally timely; b. follow-up investigations were carried out in all but one case (due to resource constraints by the municipal authority concerned) within two weeks; c. contrary to EU requirements (22), in six cases where MRL violations had been identified, only a description of the events had been presented in the follow-up file but there was no record of the origin of the non-compliance having been identified and the operator's responsibilities having been established. The audit team did acknowledge that the determination of the origin of the non- compliances had not always been possible ­ but this should nevertheless have resulted in an appropriate conclusion being documented. Furthermore, the municipal authorities did not ensure that the farms visited took adequate measures to prevent further occurrences of such non-compliances (although in a number of cases general advice was given to the pertinent sector). Prompt investigations of non-compliant residue results contribute to identifying and reducing the causes of residues in food of animal origin. citations.text: In the validation files for thyrostats, nitrofurans and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, where testing of urine and muscle was involved, no information was available on the species from which urine and muscle included in the validations had originated. The absence of this basic data undermines claims that the methods in question were appropriately validated for certain species/matrix combinations.

In all but one (beta-lactams) of the validation files scrutinised, stability was not addressed either in solution or in matrix. This is not in line with the EU legislation (28). The audit team pointed out that, if stability data are available from scientific literature or from another laboratory, these data do not need to be determined again by the concerned laboratory, provided that identical conditions apply (28).

In all, but one, of the validation files scrutinised, ruggedness was not formally addressed/assessed while the data collected allowed this to be done. This is not in line with pertinent EU requirements (28). (25) Article 39 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. (26) Article 6 and Point 7 of Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2021/808 and Article 34(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. (27) Part 2 of Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2021/808. (28) Part 2.1. of Chapter 2 of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 7

In all of the validation files scrutinised, the audit team noted that the acceptability ranges for the parameters of the calibration curves had not been described, which contradicts EU requirements (29) (see also finding 47(c)).

The audit team observed a number of cases where (within day) repeatability and (between day) reproducibility values were similar. While single values can indeed be comparable, it cannot be a systemic phenomenon due to the very nature of the repeatability and reproducibility conditions, which is reflected in EU requirements (30). The possible impact of these observations on the conclusion, that the said methods were fit for their intended use, was not commented on, or discussed in any of the validation reports seen by the audit team.

In four of the validation reports for confirmatory methods scrutinised, a number of the trueness and precision (repeatability and reproducibility) values were outside the performance criteria set by EU legislation (34). The impact of such a deviation on the intended use of the methods was neither discussed nor evaluated in the validation reports.

The audit team noted that during routine use of the method for thyrostats, there was no consideration of the instability of the analytes during freezing/thawing cycles and during storage in a freezer (35) which may undermine the validity of the results (i.e. truly non-compliant samples may not be detected).

During the validation of the steroids' method, two fortification levels were used; pertinent EU legislation requires three fortification levels (36). This omission weakens the laboratory's conclusion that the method was fit for its intended use.

citations.text: The audit team scrutinised the implementation of internal quality controls for analytical runs of five non-compliant results generated in 2019-2021 by the FFA laboratory and observed the following: a. In two cases, the difference between two parallel runs considerably exceeded the methods' within-laboratory reproducibility ­ no evaluation of the possible impact of that phenomenon on the analytical and legal validity of results was made. b. In two cases, the results obtained and reported were outside the calibration ranges without any evaluation of the possible impact on the analytical and legal validity of the results. Furthermore, this may raise a question of deviation from relevant requirements of the ISO/IEC 17025:2017 accreditation (39). c. In one case, the coefficient of determination R2 of the calibration curve was below 0.35 which normally indicates unacceptably low quality of the calibration curve (though the laboratory had no acceptability criteria for the parameters of the curve, see finding 39). However, the result was calculated on the basis of that calibration curve which may put in question the validity of the decision made on the basis of that result. d. For the screening method for antibacterial substances in milk, the audit team noted that once a suspect non-compliant result was identified, the same sample was screened again before a decision was made to confirm the screened positive result with a chemical confirmatory method. This practice may lead to the situation where non-compliant results would not be identified due to false- compliant outcome of screening testing (which could for example occur due to analyte instability in matrix), is not in line with legal requirements (40) and contradicts the bioassay manual. e. For majority of the analytical runs scrutinised, the audit team noted that no quality control charts were created and maintained at the time of the testing, although relevant and sufficient quality control samples were included. The laboratory representative clarified that, for the methods scrutinised, pertinent quality control charts were in operation since 2021, while for other methods quality control charts had been in use for a longer time. The audit team saw a number of current control charts and found that they were largely in line with EU requirements (41), although not all of the values outside the established acceptance criteria had been properly spotted and analysed in a documented traceable manner.

Notwithstanding the fact that the FFA laboratory is accredited, operates methods included in its scope of accreditation and performs well in proficiency tests, the absence of official designation of the laboratory, deficiencies in the validation of analytical methods and in the operation of internal quality controls undermine the reliability of analytical results and the subsequent enforcement decisions taken. 6. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 37. Associated findings Nos. 34 and 36.

citations.text: The FFA has not yet drawn up the required contingency plans for any of the priority pests, contrary to the requirements of Article 25(1), (4) and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

The CA has not carried out any simulation exercises concerning the implementation of the contingency plans as required by Article 26(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Nevertheless, the FFA stated that it has some experience concerning the management of outbreaks of priority pests after the successful eradication of an outbreak of Anoplophora glabripennis. 10 Conclusions on contingency plans

There is a risk of delays in applying effective and efficient measures in the case of priority pest outbreaks in Finland as none of the ten required contingency plans have been completed and no simulation exercises have been carried out. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION Since 2021, the CAs of Finland are implementing a five-year multi-annual survey programme for the 67 Union quarantine pests which have been assessed as being capable of establishing, spreading and having a significant impact within its territory. The planning of the multi-annual survey programme and annual surveys is risk based and provides a sound basis for the early detection of any outbreaks of these pests. The annual surveys for the three priority pests covered by the audit scope; Xylella fastidiosa, Agrilus planipennis and PWN provide a high level of assurance that any outbreaks of these pests will be detected promptly. There is a risk of delays in applying effective and efficient measures in the case of priority pest outbreaks as none of the ten required contingency plans have been completed and no simulation exercises have been carried out. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting between the audit team and representatives of the CA was held remotely on 29 November 2024, during which the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit team were presented. The CA offered initial comments on the findings and conclusions presented by the audit team. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authority is invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below. With regard to those non-compliances noted in the audit report which did not result in a recommendation, the competent authority is, nevertheless, invited to address these. recommendations.text: To ensure that emergency authorisations are granted in line with Article 53(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Recommendation based on conclusion No 27 Associated findings No 23 and 24

citations.text: Tukes has a rule of thumb that emergency authorisations should not be given for more than five years, but exceptions have been made and the audit team noted cases of repeated emergency authorisations for many years (e.g. in one case, 8 years, so far). The audit team considered that these applications would be more correctly accommodated within the conventional authorisation framework maintaining the system's integrity as referred to in Commission Staff Working Document on emergency situations according to Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. This is especially so because Tukes only grants emergency authorisations for PPPs that contain approved active substances, as mentioned above, and those PPPs are generally authorised already in one or more other MS.

Furthermore, the audit team noted that the CA had considered as a single emergency authorisation in 2023 a use granted for two non-consecutive periods of two months (April to May and September to October), which is not in line with Article 53 of Regulation (EC) 1107/2009. In addition, there are cases of single emergency authorisations granted for multiple crops or targets, which is also not in line with the said Article.

Emergency authorisations may each include multiple crops and/or targets or extend to a total period beyond 120 days. This is not in line with Article 53 of Regulation No (EC) 1107/2009. Furthermore, emergency authorisations generally involve approved active substances and PPPs authorised elsewhere. The dangers these authorisations are addressing could therefore, at least in the medium term, be contained by the regular authorisation procedures laid down in Articles 33, 40, or 51 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Using emergency authorisations repeatedly instead, waters down the integrity of the authorisation system. 5.2. recommendations.text: To ensure that: · The official controls include all PPP operators in the chain of marketing and use of PPPs, and are risk-based, as required by Articles 9(1) and 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, · The Competent Authority keeps an up-to-date list of operators as required by Article 10(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion No 53 Associated findings No 44, 45, 49 and 50

citations.text: As a general rule, samples are taken from distributors' warehouses and retailers. Finland aims to control about 20 PPPs annually, which is around 5% of PPPs authorised in Finland. In order to collect the samples, the only two inspectors doing controls on marketing of PPPs select the operators to be visited randomly, as they do not have operators classified based on risk. Furthermore, retailers selling only PPPs for non- professional use are usually not included. This system is not fully in line with Article 9(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Inadequate risk assessment for prioritisation of inspections was also noted in the 2014 audit.

According to information provided by Tukes inspectors, three large companies, which have approximately 130 outlets (based on the information available from open sources) supply the majority of the Finnish market of PPPs for professional use. In addition, there is an unknown number of retailers (also mainly outlets of larger chains) selling only PPPs for non-professional use. Retailers do not need to register with Tukes, so precise numbers cannot be given, and Tukes does not keep the up-to-date list of operators required by Article 10(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 10

Each centre selects the operators to be controlled for PPP use. However, the ELY centres have not been provided with risk criteria from the FFA for this. The audit team interviewed staff from three ELY centres. They stated that they select operators based on their own criteria and while they have knowledge of the farmers that receive subsidies under the Common Agricultural Policy or under other national schemes, they do not have a full overview of the universe to be controlled. In particular, the number of non- agricultural users is not known. In one ELY centre, the operators are randomly selected, in the second, the potential contamination of ground water was mentioned as a potential criterion for selection of farmers and in the third, a main crop (potatoes) cultivated in the region was a criterion for selection. This is not fully in line with Article 9(1) and (2) and Article 10(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Inadequate risk assessment for prioritisation of inspections was also noted in the 2014 audit.

Moreover, the results of the PPP residue and water status monitoring programmes are not taken into consideration for the programming of controls which is not in line with Article 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The CAs plan controls to define broad areas of controls at national level, based to an extent on risk. However, the lack of a clear and complete universe for control, the lack of risk assessment to target the relatively few inspections at regional level and the prior notifications of inspections may reduce the general effectiveness of controls. recommendations.text: To ensure that samples of PPPs are analysed to determine the presence of unacceptable co-formulants as referred to in Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and the content of impurities with a maximum content is established in the approval of relevant active substances, as referred to in Article 6(b) of the same Regulation. Such controls are required by Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion No 61 Associated findings No 58 and 59

citations.text: The analyses focus on identifying the content of active substances and certain physical and chemical properties of PPPs. They do not cover co-formulants and impurities. Consequently, the CAs are unable to verify the absence of unacceptable co-formulants in PPPs, as outlined in Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and listed in its Annex IIII. They are also unable to determine whether certain impurities exceed the maximum content permitted in the approval of the relevant active substances, as referred to in Article 6(b) of the same Regulation. This is not in line with Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The CA stated that the technical capabilities for detecting impurities, co-formulants and auxiliary substances do exist, since the laboratory is equipped with suitable analytical tools. However due to a lack of validated methods, the results cannot be reported in compliance with general standards of good laboratory practices or used for enforcement. 12

The FFA laboratory is the designated laboratory for PPP formulation analyses, and it is accredited to ISO 17025. This provides the basis for ensuring reliable results of tests and analyses. However, not including analyses for unacceptable co-formulants and regulated impurities in the sampling programme reduces the overall capability of the control system to ensure the safety of the PPPs placed on the market. 5.3. recommendations.text: To ensure that control points comply with the minimum requirements for border control posts for the categories of goods for which they have been designated and are only listed if compliant with those requirements, and that identity and physical checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin intended for human consumption and food contact materials transferred to control points are performed in the designated facilities of these control points. Legal basis: Articles 53(1)(a) and 64(3)(b) and (h) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Articles 3(1)(b) and (c) and 3(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 . Recommendation based on conclusion No. 50 Associated finding Nos. 48 and 49
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 53(1)(a) and 64(3)(b) and (h) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Articles 3(1)(b) and (c) and 3(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 . Recommendation based on conclusion No. 50 Associated finding Nos. 48 and 49

citations.text: The audit team visited four control points designated by Customs for the performance of identity and physical checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin intended for human consumption, food contact materials and plants. None of the control points visited were compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs, which is not in line with Article 53(1)(a) of the OCR and Articles 3(1)(b) and (c) and 3(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 (12). In particular, the audit team noted that: · Control point 1 had an inspection area, but without a supply of hot and cold running water and facilities for washing and drying hands, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(b) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. This control point had no storage facilities to keep goods chilled or frozen, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) of the OCR and Article 3(1)(c) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · Control point 2 had three different inspection areas, but only one inspection area had a supply of hot and cold running water and facilities for washing and drying hands. Consequently, two out of the three inspection areas were not compliant with the requirements laid down in Article 3(1)(b) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. This control point had not storage facilities to keep goods frozen, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) of the OCR and Article 3(1)(b) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · The inspection room in control point 3 was not maintained in good order and kept clean, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(h) of the OCR and Article 3(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; and · Control point 4 had an inspection area, but without a supply of hot and cold running water and facilities for washing and drying hands, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(b) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. This control point had no storage facilities to keep goods frozen, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) of the OCR and Article 3(1)(c) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. (12) In their response to the draft report, the competent authorities stated that the deficiencies in the refrigerated and frozen product facilities were due to incomplete markings in the listing of control points. Not all inspected warehouses are approved for chilled and frozen products. Customs are working to correct these errors in the list of control points. 14

The FFA and Customs informed the audit team that goods of non-animal origin entering through BCPs in Finland which are selected for identity and physical checks, including sampling, are generally forwarded to control points for the performance of these checks. However, the audit team noted that in two of these four control points visited, Customs were not using the inspection facilities for controls on consignments of goods of non- animal origin intended for human consumption and food contact materials, which is not in line with Article 53(1)(a) of the OCR. Conclusions on the compliance of border control posts with minimum requirements

The BCPs, including inspection centres thereof, were compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of animals and goods for which they had been designated, except for goods of non-animal origin intended for human consumption and food contact materials. In addition, all the four control points visited were not compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the NAP contains quantitative objectives and targets to reduce risks and impacts of pesticide use on human health and the environment, as required by Article 4(1) of Directive 2009/128/EC and timetables and reduction targets for active substances of particular concern, as required by Article 4(1), second and third subparagraphs of the same Directive. Recommendation based on conclusion No 18 Associated findings Nos 16 and 17

citations.text: Overall, the NAP III is generally comprehensive with 32 measures addressing all aspects of the SUD, some of which are new and others are updated measures from the previous NAP. These aim at reducing 1) the risk to human and animal health and the environment arising from the use of PPPs and 2) the dependency on the use of chemical PPPs. However, the audit team noted that the NAP does not contain quantitative objectives and targets to reduce risks and impacts of pesticide use on human health and the environment, which are required by Article 4(1) of the SUD. This is acknowledged by the CAs who also stated that, due to the limited availability of alternatives to the current PPPs placed on the market, during the discussions with the various stakeholders, it was decided to follow the implementation of the NAP through qualitative descriptions of the state of play of the ongoing measures, instead of monitoring the achievements of quantitative objectives and targets.

Five active substances of particular concern have been identified and the quantities sold are monitored (albeit somewhat imprecisely). The issue is closely followed up by the NAP steering group, as noted in a meeting held in May 2025, where it was agreed to work on identifying new active substances of particular concern7 (see also paragraph 72). However, the audit team noted that the NAP lacks timetables and reduction targets for these active substances. This is not in line with Article 4(1), second and third subparagraphs of the SUD. 6 https://tukes.fi/en/safe-use-of-plant-protection-products/national-action-plan-for-the-sustainable-use-of-plant- protection-products/national-action-plan-on-sustainable-plant-protection-iii-2023-2027 7 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that: `Since the audit visit in June 2025, the list of substances of particular concern has been amended. The development of appropriate indicators for substances of particular concern is further considered in the NAP steering group.' 9 Conclusions on the NAP

The current NAP, in its third version, is generally well-structured, with 32 measures addressing all aspects of the SUD and takes into account a comprehensive review, carried out between 2022 and 2023, of the achievements obtained by its second version. It represents a solid basis for the implementation of a general strategy to reduce the risk to human, animal health and the environment arising from the use of PPPs and the dependency on the use of chemical PPPs. However, it does not contain quantitative objectives and reduction targets, including timetables and reduction targets for active substances of particular concern. This reduces the capacity of the CAs to monitor the effectiveness of the general strategy of the NAP. 5.3. TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION, SALES OF PESTICIDES Legal Requirements Articles 5 and 6 of Directive 2009/128/EC Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls of professional users of PPPs pay adequate attention to enforce all relevant risk mitigation measures to protect the aquatic environment and drinking water supplies, as required by Article 11(2)(c) of Directive 2009/128/EC in conjunction with Article 55 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Recommendation based on conclusion No 44 Associated finding No 36

citations.text: The audit team noted that the afore-mentioned risk mitigation measures and restrictions are priority areas for attention in the 2025 official controls programme (see paragraph 8) and this is reflected in the revised general guidance and checklist provided to inspectors. Risk-mitigation measures and restrictions in relation to water were generally verified during the official controls observed. However, with regard to buffer zones to protect surface water, inspectors generally only verify/measure compliance with the 3 m buffer zone. In general, no controls are carried out to verify compliance when wider buffer zones are applicable, as required by the relevant PPP authorisation (as was the case for certain pesticides used by the farmers visited). It is particularly noteworthy that larger buffer zones have not been enforced during a year (2025) when the focus is water protection. As a result, the CAs are unable to ensure that all the necessary risk mitigation measures to protect water are implemented by the professional users of PPPs, as required by Article 11(2)(c) of the SUD and by Article 55 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.

Risk mitigation measures for protecting water bodies are specified as conditions for use in all PPP authorisations. These are specified on the PPP labels and are generally enforced during official controls. However, enforcement of required buffer zones to protect water bodies is limited to the general minimum measure of 3m. This enforcement is inadequate when larger buffer zones are necessary, which does not ensure the overall level of water protection.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls of professional users pay adequate attention to the way PPPs are prepared before use and the cleaning of PAE after use, as required by Article 13(1) of Directive 2009/128/EC. Recommendation based on conclusion No 55 Associated findings Nos 4, 7 and 54

citations.text: BACKGROUND 4.1. LEGAL CONTEXT AND ACTIONS TAKEN BY THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION The 2006 Thematic Strategy on the sustainable use of pesticides led to a new legislative framework for the approval and use of pesticides. This includes a strict framework for the approval of active substances by the European Commission and the authorisation of PPPs by MS, introduced by Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, adopted on 21 October 2009. This 2 Regulation requires that active substances may be approved, and PPPs be authorised, only if they have no identified harmful effects on human and animal health, and no unacceptable effects on the environment. It also requires that PPPs be applied according to their authorised conditions of use. The SUD was adopted on the same date (21 October 2009) as part of the above-mentioned Thematic Strategy. It should be noted that the SUD applies to pesticides that are PPPs according to its Article 2(1) and point 10(a) of Article 3. As the SUD employs the term `pesticides,' in the report this term is used as appropriate when referring to the SUD. Article 4 of the SUD requires MS to adopt National Action Plans (NAPs) to set up quantitative objectives, targets, measures and timetables to reduce risks and impacts of pesticide use and to encourage the development and introduction of integrated pest management (IPM) and of alternative approaches or techniques in order to reduce dependency on the use of pesticides. In addition, the NAPs must also include indicators to monitor the use of PPPs containing active substances of particular concern, especially if alternatives are available. NAPs must be reviewed at least every five years, and any substantial changes must be reported to the Commission without undue delay. The SUD also identifies specific actions that MS are required to include in their NAPs for proper implementation. The main actions relate to training of users, advisors and distributors, inspection of PAE, the prohibition of aerial spraying, limiting pesticide use in sensitive areas, and information and awareness-raising about pesticide risks. A cornerstone of the SUD is the promotion and implementation of IPM, for which general principles are laid down in its Annex III. Article 55 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 requires PPPs to be used properly. This means the application of the principles of good plant protection practice and compliance with the conditions established in accordance with Article 31 of the same Regulation and specified on the label. In addition, Article 55 also stipulates that proper use includes compliance with the provisions of the SUD and, in particular, with the general principles of IPM, as referred to in Article 14 and Annex III to the SUD. In this regard, Article 14(4) of the SUD requires that the NAP includes a description of how the CAs ensure that the general principles of IPM are implemented by professional users of PPPs. In addition, the European Court of Auditors, in its Special Report 05/20201, highlighted the need to convert the general principles of IPM into practical and measurable criteria2. Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 requires MS to carry out official controls in order to verify compliance with the rules referred to in its Article 1(2), including requirements for the placing on the market and use of PPPs and the sustainable use of pesticides, with the exception of PAE. 1 https://www.eca.europa.eu/en/publications/SR20_05 2 Recommendation 1(a) of the report requires the Commission to check that MSs convert the general IPM principles into practical and measurable criteria and that they verify these criteria at farm level. 3 The Commission submitted its second report to the European Parliament and the Council on the experience gained by MS on the implementation of national targets established in their NAPs and on progress in the implementation of the SUD in May 2020. Compared with CAP conditionality controls, the PPP/SUD specific official controls also include the verification of compliance with the use of PPPs as laid down by Article 55 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, and with the general principles of IPM, set out by Annex III to the SUD. Given the scope and objectives of the audit, the audit team paid more attention to these official controls. On an annual basis, the FFA defines a risk- based theme and allocates the number of controls to each ELY centre. Overall, between 80 to 100 of professional users of PPPs are subject to these controls annually. Each ELY centre selects the various operators to inspect taking into account the annual theme and the instructions included in a general control guidance, which is reviewed every year by the FFA. Furthermore, a checklist to be used during the inspections is also attached to the control guidance. These documents offer a solid foundation for local inspectors at ELY centres to conduct official controls. However, they do not adequately focus on the preparation of PPPs before use and the cleaning of PAE after use (see paragraph 54).

During the inspections at professional users, the audit team noted that the storage conditions are generally verified. However, operations such as the preparation of PPPs 17 before use and cleaning of PAE after use are generally not verified, or are only superficially checked, and are not included in the inspection checklist. This does not allow the CA to ensure that these operations are carried out without endangering human health and the environment, as laid down by Article 13(1) of the SUD. Conclusions on handling and storage of pesticides

Clear instructions for safe storing and disposal are given on the label of all PPPs and on the Tukes website. The collection of PPP packaging and remnants is well organised and verified by the municipalities. Nonetheless, during official controls, certain aspects like the safe preparation of PPPs and the cleaning of PAE after use are generally not checked. This reduces the ability of the CA to ensure the necessary protection of the health of professional users of PPPs and the environment. 5.8. citations.text: During the observed controls, the audit team noted that the verification of the implementation of IPM general principles, was superficial. The interviews tended to be more advisory rather than compliance-focused, which is corroborated by the limited and general indications outlined in the control guidance. For instance, when asked if preventive methods and control measures are used to manage pests by monitoring pest presence, a simple 'yes' response, such as 'yes, there are preventive measures and we monitor pest presence', would typically be recorded as 'YES' without further probing. Additionally, the audit team observed inconsistencies among inspectors from different ELY centres. As an example, one inspector may place more emphasis on recording pest monitoring results, while another may prioritise documenting the success of plant protection measures. This approach, which is linked to the lack of practical and measurable criteria to assess and enforce the implementation of the general principles of IPM, does not ensure that the general principles of IPM are implemented by professional users of PPPs as required by Article 55 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Moreover, the audit team noted that the NAP does not include a description of how the CAs ensure that the general principles of IPM are implemented by professional users of PPPs. This is not in line with Article14(4) of the SUD

The application of IPM general principles as laid down by Annex III to the SUD is obligatory for all professional users and a wide and comprehensive range of measures to promote IPM and organic agriculture, including IPM crop specific guidelines and pest monitoring and forecasting tools for professional users, are described in the current NAP. Nonetheless, the absence of a description of how the CAs ensure that the general principles of IPM are implemented by professional users of PPPs in the NAP and, in particular, the lack of any practical criteria establishing the minimum requirements that professional users of PPPs should meet in order to fulfil their obligations as regard the general principles of IPM, does not facilitate effective implementation by all professional users and does not provide a clear basis for effective enforcement. 19 https://www.ruokavirasto.fi/elintarvikkeet/elintarvikeala/tuote--ja-toimialakohtaiset- vaatimukset/luomuelintarvikkeet/valvonta/luomusertifikaatti/ 21 5.9.
